verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “five days ago I started having problems like a cough and my nose is just constantly streaming” and later confirms “Yeah, five days or so ago.”

When asked, “Are you bringing up any phlegm at all?” patient replies, “No, no.”
Doctor asks, “Any pain in your chest?” Patient answers, “No.”
Doctor asks about “Any difficulty breathing, feeling short of breath?” Patient responds, “No, that's all fine.”
Doctor: “Have you coughed up any blood or anything like that?” Patient: “Nope.” (i.e., no haemoptysis).
Patient says, “I've been feeling really hot… sometimes I'm feeling really chilly,” and when asked, “Have you checked your temperature with a thermometer?” replies, “No, I haven't.”
Doctor: “Vomiting, diarrhea now?” Patient: “No.”
Patient: “around when it started. I had some diarrhea, but I don't know if that was associated. But since then it's all been pretty fine.”
Doctor: “And are you eating and drinking normally?” Patient: “Yes,” and later confirms fluids: “Yeah.”

Patient: “I've had quite achy muscles, but that's pretty much it.”

Patient: “metformin and lisinopril, I think, is the other one.”

No discussion is documented about changing or not changing metformin or lisinopril doses or regimens.

Patient: “My partner and my dog.” in response to “Who do you live with at home?”
Patient: “Yes, I'm an office manager.”

You probably have got an infection in the chest… you’re obviously getting the symptoms of your nose and your chest… Most of the time these infections are caused by viruses, so they do normally settle by themselves.” This aligns with an acute likely viral respiratory infection with dry cough and nasal symptoms.
Doctor explicitly mentions “infection in the chest… symptoms of your nose and your chest,” indicating possible chest involvement.

Hypertension is a known chronic problem discussed (“I've got hypertension”) and remains part of the medical context; it is reasonable as an active problem, and nothing suggests it is resolved.

Doctor: “it’s definitely worth getting a thermometer and checking your temperature.” Patient asks about getting one at a pharmacy and doctor agrees.

Doctor: “if the temperature is ongoing above 37.5, 38, you keep spiking temperatures… or your cough's getting worse, you're coughing up lots of nasty phlegm… or any shortness of breath, chest pain, then we certainly would need to speak to you again.”
Doctor: “It's fine to carry on what you're doing at the moment with the lemcip… that contains paracetamol, so don't take any other paracetamol containing products with that at the same time.”
Doctor: “the cough syrup isn't advisable in the daytime… But if you're kept up all night and you can't sleep at all, then it's okay to have a little bit of cough syrup just to settle that down.”
There is no explicit advice in the transcript about maintaining hydration or resting, even though it’s implied by context.
Doctor: “Most of the time. These infections are caused by viruses, so they do normally settle by themselves… it can take, you know, a week or two.”

Doctor advises recontact if persistent fever, worsening cough, “coughing up lots of nasty phlegm” (purulent sputum), “cough up any blood,” “blood coming out your nose,” or “shortness of breath, chest pain,” at which point “we would need to speak to you again” and had earlier discussed possible antibiotics if not settling.
Doctor: “make sure that you have the regular diabetes and blood pressure checkups that your GP has asked you for.” Also asks if patient has blood sugar checking equipment.

Doctor: “Do you have blood sugar checking equipment?” Patient: “I'm not at home, no.” Doctor then emphasizes ensuring regular diabetes and BP checkups with GP; using a home monitor “if available” vs relying on GP is implied and consistent.
Transcript does not include advice to avoid smoking (just notes she does not smoke) or to maintain hydration or explicitly to continue regular activities as tolerated.
There is no explicit statement about making or not making changes to metformin or lisinopril therapy.

Follow-up advice mentions fever, worsening cough, purulent sputum, hemoptysis, chest pain, shortness of breath, or blood from nose, but there is no mention of wheeze, confusion, or inability to keep fluids down.
